core-devops-concepts.description: The vocabulary every DevOps interview opens with: what DevOps actually changes, why it exists, and how CI, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment differ.
study_notes: Can you define DevOps without listing tools?
The precise boundary between continuous delivery and continuous deployment.
Which business metrics improve, and how you would measure them.

docker.description: Container fundamentals - images versus containers, Dockerfile authoring, Compose, and the client/daemon architecture underneath `docker run`.
study_notes: Image layers, the build cache, and how to keep images small.
Why a container is not a virtual machine.
Multi-stage builds and running as a non-root user.

kubernetes.description: The control plane, the workload objects you touch daily, and the networking abstractions that make Pods reachable.
study_notes: What each control-plane component does when you run `kubectl apply`.
Service types and when each is appropriate.
Why Pods are ephemeral and what that implies for state.

cicd.description: Pipeline design, Jenkins and GitLab CI mechanics, and the delivery-versus-deployment distinction interviewers love to test.
study_notes: Stages of a pipeline you have actually built, in order.
How you keep pipelines fast and trustworthy.
Where secrets and artifacts live in your pipeline.

cloud-platforms.description: Cloud service models and the three major providers - enough breadth to discuss AWS, Azure, and GCP comparatively.
study_notes: IaaS / PaaS / SaaS boundaries and the shared responsibility model.
Equivalent services across AWS, Azure, and GCP.
Regions, availability zones, and how they shape architecture.

infrastructure-as-code.description: Declarative infrastructure with Terraform and Ansible - state, providers, idempotency, and where each tool belongs.
study_notes: Provisioning versus configuration management.
How you manage Terraform state safely in a team.
What makes a change idempotent.

monitoring-and-logging.description: Metrics, logs, and the toolchain - Prometheus, Grafana, and the ELK stack - plus the conceptual split between monitoring and logging.
study_notes: Pull versus push metric collection.
What you alert on versus what you only dashboard.
How logs get from a container to a searchable index.

security-and-compliance.description: Shifting security left: DevSecOps practice, infrastructure and container hardening, and compliance expressed as code.
study_notes: Where security gates belong in a pipeline, and what fails the build.
How you handle secrets and image vulnerabilities.
Turning a control framework into automated checks.

linux-administration.description: The operating system under everything - commands, shell scripting, systemd, service management, and the filesystem hierarchy.
study_notes: Diagnosing a slow or full host from the shell alone.
Writing a safe, idempotent shell script.
How systemd starts, supervises, and logs a service.

version-control.description: Git mechanics and the branching models teams actually argue about, including how to resolve conflicts calmly.
study_notes: Git Flow versus trunk-based development, and which suits continuous deployment.
Merge versus rebase, and when each is safe.
How you recover from a bad merge or a force push.

configuration-management.description: Keeping fleets consistent with Puppet, Chef, Ansible, and Salt - push versus pull, agent versus agentless.
study_notes: Desired state, drift, and convergence.
Trade-offs between the major tools.
Where configuration management ends and immutable infrastructure begins.

scalability-and-high-availability.description: Designing systems that grow and stay up: scaling dimensions, load balancing, auto scaling, and recovery objectives.
study_notes: Vertical versus horizontal scaling and the limits of each.
Load-balancing algorithms and health checks.
The difference between high availability and disaster recovery.

backup-and-disaster-recovery.description: Backup types, RPO/RTO targets, business continuity planning, and the discipline of testing restores.
study_notes: The 3-2-1 rule and why an untested backup is not a backup.
Deriving RPO and RTO from business requirements.
Costs and trade-offs of DR patterns from backup-restore to active-active.

cloud-native-architecture.description: Microservices, service mesh, event-driven design, and the Twelve-Factor principles that make apps portable.
study_notes: When a microservice split helps and when it hurts.
How a mesh changes the responsibilities of application code.
Config, state, and logs as Twelve-Factor treats them.

performance-testing.description: Load, stress, soak, and spike testing - how to design them, which tools to use, and how to read the results.
study_notes: Percentiles versus averages when reporting latency.
How you build a realistic workload model.
Turning a test result into a capacity decision.

api-gateway-and-service-mesh.description: The API edge: gateway responsibilities, security, rate limiting, and documentation as a first-class artifact.
study_notes: Gateway versus load balancer versus service mesh.
Token-bucket rate limiting and how limits are communicated to clients.
OAuth 2.0, OIDC, and where validation happens.

container-orchestration-advanced.description: Beyond Deployments - StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Helm packaging, Istio, and the container runtime interface.
study_notes: Why stateful workloads need stable identity and storage.
How Helm templating and releases work, including rollback.
What replaced Docker as the kubelet's runtime, and why.

devops-tools-and-automation.description: GitOps with Argo CD, Tekton pipelines, and the deployment strategies used to ship without downtime.
study_notes: Push-based CD versus pull-based GitOps reconciliation.
Choosing between blue/green, canary, and rolling deploys.
How drift is detected and corrected automatically.

cloud-cost-optimization.description: Reserved and spot capacity, tagging discipline, and the reports that turn a cloud bill into accountable engineering work.
study_notes: Commitment options and their break-even points.
Designing workloads that tolerate spot interruption.
Making cost visible to the teams that create it.

site-reliability-engineering.description: Google's operational model: SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, and the systematic elimination of toil.
study_notes: Writing an SLI that reflects user experience.
What an exhausted error budget should actually change.
Which work counts as toil and how you cap it.

devops-metrics-and-kpis.description: The four DORA metrics and the measurement habits that keep them honest.
study_notes: Definitions of deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, and MTTR.
How teams game each metric, and how to prevent it.
Which metric you would improve first, and why.

serverless-architecture.description: Functions as a service, the operational model behind them, and the design patterns that keep serverless workloads fast and cheap.
study_notes: Cold starts and how to mitigate them.
Statelessness, idempotency, and event-source semantics.
When serverless is the wrong choice.

database-management-in-devops.description: Treating schemas as code: version control, migration tooling, backup strategy, and performance tuning.
study_notes: Running an online schema change with zero downtime.
Expand/contract migrations and backward compatibility.
Reading a slow query plan and acting on it.

network-security.description: Zero trust, TLS, web application firewalls, and segmentation - the controls that protect traffic in and between clouds.
study_notes: The TLS handshake and what certificate validation proves.
Zero trust as an architecture, not a product.
Segmentation at the network and Kubernetes-policy levels.

incident-management.description: Detection through post-mortem: response plans, severity levels, on-call practice, and blameless learning.
study_notes: Roles during an incident and who declares severity.
What a good post-mortem produces beyond a document.
Designing an on-call rotation people can sustain.

devops-culture-and-practices.description: The human half of DevOps - shared ownership, blamelessness, knowledge sharing, and collaboration that survives incidents.
study_notes: How you would change a team that treats operations as someone else's job.
Making a post-incident review genuinely blameless.
Documentation practices that outlive their authors.

infrastructure-monitoring.description: Host and platform monitoring, APM, log management, and the practices that keep dashboards and alerts useful.
study_notes: The USE and RED methods for choosing what to measure.
Distributed tracing and where it beats logs.
Alert fatigue and how to design it away.

cloud-migration.description: Assessment, the 6 Rs, application modernization, and the tooling that moves workloads without surprises.
study_notes: Picking a migration strategy per application, not per portfolio.
How you cut over with minimal downtime and a rollback plan.
Discovery and dependency mapping before any move.

advanced-devops-cloud.description: Senior-level ground: platform engineering, FinOps, policy as code, chaos engineering, observability, and progressive delivery.
study_notes: Treating the internal platform as a product with users.
Designing a chaos experiment with a hypothesis and a blast radius.
Automating governance so policy is enforced, not asked for.

devsecops.description: Security built into the delivery pipeline: scanning layers, SBOMs and supply-chain provenance, image signing, secretless pipelines, and vulnerability triage that does not stall delivery.
study_notes: Which gates block a build, and how you handle the existing backlog.
SBOM, provenance, and signature verification that fails closed.
Ranking vulnerabilities by exploitability and exposure, not CVSS alone.

secops.description: Security operations for engineers: SOC workflow, SIEM and normalisation, detection engineering, MITRE ATT&CK coverage, threat hunting, and security incident response.
study_notes: Detecting behaviour rather than artifacts, and validating the detection.
Preserving evidence before containment during a security incident.
Which telemetry you would onboard first, and why identity logs come top.

slo-engineering.description: The engineering practice behind SLOs: choosing targets, burn-rate alerting, correct latency SLIs, error budget policies, and SLOs for batch, async, and third-party dependencies.
study_notes: Multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting, and why the short window exists.
Latency as a threshold ratio rather than a percentile value.
Owning the SLO even when the failing dependency is not yours.

sla-management.description: The commercial side of reliability: SLA versus SLO versus OLA, downtime and composite availability arithmetic, contract clauses, service credits, reporting, and breach response.
study_notes: Allowed downtime per target, and composite availability across dependencies.
Why measurement definitions and exclusions cause more disputes than the number.
What you do - commercially and technically - when you breach.

aws-engineering.description: Depth on AWS: VPC design, IAM policy evaluation, ECS/EKS/Fargate, Auto Scaling with load balancers, S3 storage classes, highly available databases, multi-account organisations, and IaC choices.
study_notes: How IAM evaluates a request, including SCPs and cross-account access.
Why the account is the blast-radius boundary.
Making an application survive a database failover.

azure-engineering.description: Depth on Azure: the resource hierarchy, Entra ID and RBAC, VNet and private endpoint design, AKS, Bicep, Azure Policy and landing zones, Azure Monitor with KQL, and the compute options.
study_notes: Management groups, subscriptions, and resource groups - what each bounds.
Private endpoints and the private DNS configuration they depend on.
Azure Policy effects, and rolling out Deny without breaking teams.

gcp-engineering.description: Depth on Google Cloud: resource hierarchy and org policies, IAM without service-account keys, the global VPC, GKE Standard versus Autopilot, Cloud Run, Cloud Operations, IaC, and the data services.
study_notes: Why a global VPC changes multi-region design.
Workload Identity Federation instead of service-account keys.
Choosing between Cloud SQL, Spanner, and BigQuery by requirement.

cloud-engineering.description: Provider-neutral cloud engineering: landing zones, hybrid connectivity, least-privilege identity, multi-region resilience, multi-cloud trade-offs, DNS and global routing, and cross-provider service mapping.
study_notes: Right-sizing a landing zone instead of copying the enterprise template.
Recovery objectives first, then the cheapest pattern that meets them.
Translating fluently between AWS, Azure, and GCP - including where it breaks.

platform-engineering.description: Building the internal platform as a product: IDPs, golden paths, Backstage, Crossplane, self-service environments, adoption metrics, and safe rollout of breaking platform changes.
study_notes: Golden paths that are chosen, not mandated - and escapable abstractions.
Measuring adoption and developer outcomes rather than components shipped.
Versioning the platform interface and automating consumer migrations.

scripting-and-automation.description: The scripting layer under every pipeline - defensive Bash for orchestration, and Python for cloud APIs, structured data, and the tooling Bash cannot carry.
study_notes: What `set -euo pipefail` does, line by line.
Whether your script is safe to run twice.
When you stop writing Bash and reach for Python.

interview-experience.description: How the interview itself works - the round structure, explaining your project, answering scenario questions, and the company-by-company record of what was actually asked across 85 employers.
study_notes: A rehearsed 90-second walkthrough of your current project.
A justification for every technology choice you name.
A method for scenario questions that ends in prevention, not just a fix.
The specific questions your target company has actually asked before.
